Appearance and adult size

Congo African greys have pale grey feathers, a contrasting pale face, a dark bill and a vivid red tail. Timneh parrots are usually smaller and darker, with a horn-coloured upper bill and a deeper maroon tail. These are useful clues, but age, feather condition and individual variation mean that an appearance alone is not a substitute for confirming the bird's identity.

The total length is commonly around 28–36 cm, measured from bill to tail; a Congo is usually at the larger end and a Timneh at the smaller end. These active parrots need room to climb, stretch and move.

Lifespan, temperament and routine

African Grey Parrots may live for several decades, and a 30–50-year planning range is a broad guide rather than a prediction. Long-term care planning should include changes in a household, a dependable future-care arrangement and the continuing cost of food, suitable equipment and routine care.

Many greys are observant and deliberate about new people or objects. Some seek close company; others prefer interaction on their own terms. A steady daily rhythm, patient introductions and attention to posture, feather position and vocal cues help people respond without forcing contact. Sensitivity is not a defect, but it makes a calm, predictable environment especially valuable.

Noise, communication and learning

Greys can whistle, call, imitate household sounds and sometimes develop spoken words, but vocabulary and frequency are individual and cannot be promised. Calls may be sharp or persistent, particularly when a bird is excited or seeking contact. Consider how sound will carry through your home and affect neighbours before deciding that a clever parrot will be a quiet one.

Their problem-solving reputation reflects a need for mental work, not an expectation that every bird will perform tricks. Short, reward-based sessions can teach comfortable stationing, stepping onto a perch or entering a carrier. Keep requests achievable and end positively; repeated pressure or punishment can damage trust and does not replace daily opportunities to investigate and forage.

Food, housing and exercise

Build meals around a balanced, species-appropriate diet, commonly including suitable formulated food and a considered range of vegetables, with fruit and richer treats offered thoughtfully. Food preferences can be narrow, so any change should be gradual and planned with appropriate professional guidance rather than made abruptly. Fresh water and regular observation of what is actually eaten matter as much as what is offered.

Provide a secure, roomy enclosure with varied perches and enough usable space to climb and spread the wings, plus supervised time to move outside it in a parrot-safe area. Rotate safe chewing, shredding and foraging activities. Protect the bird from household hazards and plan an arrangement that allows exercise every day rather than relying on occasional out-of-cage sessions.

Social needs, enrichment and household fit

A grey needs social contact alongside the ability to occupy itself. Build independence with food-search games, destructible materials and predictable periods of quiet, so human attention is not the bird's only source of stimulation. A second bird is not an automatic solution: compatibility, separate resources and careful introductions require planning, and individual birds may not choose to share space.

First-time owners should be prepared to study body language, set a consistent routine and arrange support before taking on a long-lived, perceptive parrot. Families can provide a rewarding home when adults supervise interactions, children are taught not to grab or crowd the bird, and the parrot has a quiet retreat. Household members need to agree on the daily workload.

Behavioural challenges and lifelong commitment

Biting, alarm calls, reluctance around handling or repetitive behaviour can arise for different reasons; none should be dismissed as simple naughtiness or assumed to have one quick fix. Review routine, sleep, stimulation and the bird's environment, and seek suitable qualified advice when a concern persists. A thoughtful match and realistic expectations reduce avoidable stress for both bird and household.

Before committing, picture ordinary weekdays as well as holidays: who provides interaction, cleaning, enrichment and care if the main owner is away or unable to continue? The answer should be practical for decades, not dependent on a bird talking, cuddling on demand or remaining unchanged as it matures.
